MAPWhere the MPNs sit among blood cancers

LO 1Normal hematopoiesis: myeloid vs lymphoid

Q1. How are blood disorders studied?
  • Clinical suspicion → lab data (CBC, peripheral smear) → lymph node assessment (imaging, biopsy) → bone marrow (aspirate + biopsy)
  • Ancillary tests: flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry, cytochemistry, cytogenetics, FISH, PCR, next-generation sequencing

Marrow biopsy (core)

  • Best for cellularity
  • Pattern of focal processes (metastases, lymphoma)
  • Stroma (fibrosis)

Marrow aspirate (fluid)

  • Morphology of individual cells
  • Differential counts

Site: posterior iliac crest. Indications: definitive diagnosis of most hematologic diseases; fever of unknown origin; some infections.

Normal child

  • Mostly cells, little fat

Elderly adult

  • Mostly fat (cellularity ≈ 100 − age)

Leukemia

  • Packed, ~100% cellular
Q2. Which cells are myeloid and which are lymphoid?

Myeloid

  • Granulocytes (mostly neutrophils; eosinophils, basophils), monocytes
  • Red cells and platelets (megakaryocytes) too
  • Stimulus → reactive increase; precursor mutation → MPN

Lymphoid

  • B, T and NK cells
  • Originate in marrow; T cells mature in thymus
  • B and T cells are not distinguishable by morphology (need CD markers)

Myeloid vs lymphoid

  • Both arise from the blood stem cell

Myelopoiesis

  • Stages visible by morphology
Trap

"Myeloid" isn't just white cells: RBCs and platelets are myeloid too. That's why PV and ET are myeloid neoplasms.

Q3. How do leukemia, lymphoma, acute and chronic differ?
  • Leukemia: mainly marrow + circulating tumor cells. Lymphoma: discrete tissue masses in lymph nodes or extranodal sites (Hodgkin, non-Hodgkin B or T)
AcuteChronic
CellsImmature "blasts"Mature and maturing cells
PathogenesisMaturation arrestIncreased proliferation
ClinicalEarly marrow failure: bleeding, infections, fatigueNon-specific; organ infiltration; marked leukocytosis; late marrow failure
TreatmentUrgentNon-urgent

Oncoproteins in white cell neoplasms (non-random translocations, acquired mutations): block maturation, turn on growth signaling, alter the epigenome, inhibit apoptosis, impair tumor suppressors.

In-house exam

Myeloid disease manifestations depend on where in differentiation the transformed cell sits and how the mutation affects differentiation. Myeloid diseases can overlap and evolve into one another with extra mutations.

ApplyLO 1 application questions

A1Which marrow specimen is best for cellularity, and which for a differential count?
Biopsy for cellularity and pattern; aspirate for morphology and differential.

LO 2Reactive vs neoplastic neutrophilia

Q1. What raises or lowers the white count?

Leukocytosis (↑)

  • Reactive: infection, inflammatory disorders, drugs
  • Neoplastic

Leukopenia (↓)

  • Inherited or acquired immunodeficiency
  • Drugs, infections, malnutrition

The peripheral count depends on the marrow storage pool, the rate of release, the fraction marginated on vessel walls, and the rate of extravasation into tissue.

Causes by cell type

  • Basophilia is rare → think MPN (CML)
Step 1

Steroids and epinephrine demarginate neutrophils → ↑ count without infection.

Q2. How do I tell infection-driven neutrophilia from CML?
Reactive (infection)Neoplastic (CML)
WBC<30 ×10⁹/L>50 ×10⁹/L (50–400)
Left shiftBandsAll precursor forms (myelocytes → blasts)
BasophilsAbsentAbsolute basophilia
SpleenNot enlargedSplenomegaly
FeverYesNo
GeneticsNormalt(9;22)
High yield

Basophilia + splenomegaly + every stage of maturation + no fever = CML until proven otherwise.

Step 1

LAP score (leukocyte alkaline phosphatase): high in a leukemoid reaction, low in CML. Leukemoid reaction may show toxic granulation and Döhle bodies.

ApplyLO 2 application question

A1WBC 180,000 with myelocytes, bands and 8% basophils; no fever; spleen palpable. Reactive or neoplastic, and which test?
Neoplastic (CML) → BCR-ABL by PCR/FISH or karyotype for t(9;22).

LO 3What is a myeloproliferative neoplasm?

Q1. What do all MPNs share?
  • Mutated, constitutively activated tyrosine kinases
  • Clonal proliferation in the marrow of one or more myeloid lineages (granulocytic, erythroid, megakaryocytic)
  • Maturation is effective → high peripheral counts
  • Extramedullary hematopoiesis → splenomegaly, hepatomegaly
  • Variable "spent phase" (marrow fibrosis) and transformation to acute leukemia

Tyrosine kinase = enzyme that moves a phosphate from ATP to a tyrosine on a target protein, switching it on without external regulation → promotes growth and survival but does not impair differentiation.

In-house exam

Tyrosine kinases promote growth and survival but do NOT impair differentiation; that's why MPN cells mature and counts go up.

Analogy — the stuck accelerator

An MPN is a factory with the accelerator stuck down but a normal assembly line: too many finished products. Acute leukemia is a broken assembly line: half-built parts (blasts) pile up.

Q2. What are the four MPNs?
MPNLineage that dominatesDriver
Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML)NeutrophilsBCR-ABL, t(9;22)
Polycythemia vera (PV)Red cellsJAK2 >97%
Essential thrombocytosis (ET)Platelets (megakaryocytes)JAK2 50–60%, CALR 30%, MPL 5–10%
Primary (chronic idiopathic) myelofibrosisMegakaryocytes → fibrosisJAK2, CALR or MPL ≈90%
Memory tool

One lineage each: CML = Cells that fight (neutrophils) · PV = Plethora (red) · ET = Excess platelets · PMF = Packed with Fibers.

LO 4The four MPNs: features, mechanism, genetics

Q1. CML: how does t(9;22) cause it?
  • Most common MPN
  • t(9;22)(q34;q11) reciprocal in 95% → Philadelphia chromosome
  • Fuses BCR (chr 22) with ABL proto-oncogene (chr 9) → chimeric BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase → phosphorylates many downstream effectors
  • Result: ↑ proliferation, stem cell expansion, delayed apoptosis, premature release of immature granulocytes
  • Adults (25–60, median 55): gradual fatigue, weight loss, night sweats; abdominal discomfort / early satiety from splenomegaly

Massive splenomegaly

  • Early satiety, abdominal fullness

CML blood and marrow

  • Neutrophils at every stage + basophils; hypercellular marrow
In-house exam

59-year-old man, tired, early satiety → CML. Ph chromosome = BCR (chr 22) + ABL (chr 9) → always-on kinase.

Memory tool

"Philadelphia CreaML cheese": t(9;22) → CML. "9 to 22 is a long shift, so you're always on."

Q2. Polycythemia vera: why too many red cells?
  • Proliferation of all myeloid lines, but erythroid dominant; maturation intact; independent of normal erythropoiesis controls
  • JAK2 in >97%: valine → phenylalanine (V617F) in the JAK/STAT pathway, downstream of the EPO receptor → growth-factor independent; less potent kinase than BCR-ABL
  • ¼ have two mutated JAK2 copies → higher WBC, more organomegaly, pruritus, more spent-phase progression
  • Mean age 60; symptoms from ↑ red cell mass and abnormal flow: venous stasis, thrombosis, hemorrhage (abnormal platelet function), hypertension, headache, weakness, sweating, intense pruritus, ↑ peptic ulcer disease
  • Hb 14–28 g/dL; Hct >60%

PV smear

  • Packed red cells
In-house exam

68-year-old man with headache, dizziness and hypertension → PV. Symptoms: headache, weakness, sweating, dizziness.

Step 1

Aquagenic pruritus (itch after a hot shower, histamine from basophils), erythromelalgia, Budd-Chiari (hepatic vein thrombosis). EPO is low in PV but high in secondary polycythemia.

Q3. Essential thrombocytosis: what drives it?
  • Clonal MPN of the megakaryocytic lineage; the least common MPN
  • JAK2 50–60% · CALR 30% (activates the thrombopoietin receptor) · MPL 5–10% (the TPO receptor itself)
  • Sustained platelets >600 ×10⁹/L; large, mature megakaryocytes in marrow
  • Insidious, age 50–60: thrombosis (MI, stroke), bleeding (GI; weakness, fatigue), or asymptomatic; splenomegaly in 30–60%
  • Too many and dysfunctional platelets → both clots and bleeds

ET smear

  • Too many platelets, clumping

Abnormal platelets

  • Giant, odd shapes

ET marrow

  • Clusters of large, weird megakaryocytes
In-house exam

56-year-old woman with fatigue and erythromelalgia (burning, red hands/feet from platelet microthrombi) → ET.

Q4. Primary myelofibrosis: how does the marrow scar?
  • Obliterative marrow fibrosis + significant extramedullary hematopoiesis → splenomegaly
  • Most common >60; slow onset; splenomegaly or anemia (fatigue, weight loss, bleeding); hyperuricemia (↑ turnover)
  • Early: WBC and platelets ↑ (marked thrombocytosis), mild spleen; late: progressive leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, worsening anemia, marked spleen ± liver

Leukoerythroblastosis

  • Teardrops (dacrocytes), nucleated RBCs, granulocyte precursors

Marrow fibrosis

  • Collagen replaces cells

Liver EMH

  • Sinusoids filled with hematopoietic cells
In-house exam

Liver biopsy with hematopoietic cells in the sinusoids = extramedullary hematopoiesis (PMF). Megakaryocyte PDGF and TGF-β drive the fibrosis.

Memory tool

Teardrop logic: RBCs get squeezed out of a scarred marrow, so they "cry."

Step 1

Aspirate is a "dry tap"; reticulin/trichrome stains show fibrosis. JAK2 inhibitor ruxolitinib shrinks the spleen.

ApplyLO 4 application questions

A1Which MPN has a mutation in the thrombopoietin receptor itself?
MPL mutations: ET (5–10%) and PMF.
A2Why do PV patients both clot and bleed?
Thick blood → stasis and thrombosis; platelets are abnormal → hemorrhage.

LO 5The work-up for each MPN

Q1. Which tests confirm each MPN?
MPNBloodMarrowMolecular
CMLWBC 50–400 ×10⁹/L, all granulocytic stages, basophiliaHypercellular, maturing granulocytes, ↑ megakaryocytesBCR-ABL: karyotype t(9;22), FISH, PCR
PVHb 14–28, Hct >60%; ± ↑ WBC, platelets; low EPOPanmyelosis (erythroid + megakaryocytic)JAK2
ETPlatelets >600k, large, odd shapes, clumpingClusters of large atypical megakaryocytesJAK2, CALR, MPL; rule out BCR-ABL
PMFLeukoerythroblastosis, dacrocytes, ovalocytesFibrosis, ↓ cellularity (late)JAK2, CALR, MPL
PV WHO criteria (in-house)
MajorRed cell mass >25% above predicted · no cause of secondary erythrocytosis · splenomegaly · clonal abnormality other than Ph
MinorPlatelets >400 ×10⁹/L · WBC >12 ×10⁹/L · marrow panmyelosis · low serum EPO
High yield

ET and PMF are partly diagnoses of exclusion: always rule out BCR-ABL (CML) and reactive causes first.

LO 6Matching labs, clinic and morphology

Q1. Which picture goes with which MPN?
Stem says…Think
Fatigue, early satiety, huge spleen, WBC 150k, basophilsCML
Headache, dizziness, HTN, ruddy, itch after showering, Hct >60%, low EPOPV
Erythromelalgia, stroke or MI, GI bleed, platelets >600kET
Older adult, fatigue, abdominal fullness, infections, teardrops + nucleated RBCs, dry tapPMF
CML patient with new lymphadenopathy or blastsBlast crisis (acute transformation)
In-house exam

CML has no lymphadenopathy in chronic phase; new lymphadenopathy signals transition to the acute phase (blast crisis).

LO 7Differential diagnosis

Q1. What else causes each picture?
MPNDifferentialTie-breaker
CMLLeukemoid / reactive neutrophilia (infection, drugs, steroids)<30k, bands only, fever, no basophils, no spleen, normal genetics (high LAP)
PVSecondary polycythemia: hypoxia (COPD, altitude, smoking), EPO-secreting tumors (RCC, HCC); relative (dehydration)EPO high in secondary, low in PV; O₂ sat; JAK2
ETReactive thrombocytosis: iron deficiency, inflammation, infection, splenectomy, cancer; other MPNsLow ferritin or high CRP → reactive; BCR-ABL negative
PMFOther causes of marrow fibrosis or leukoerythroblastosis: metastatic carcinoma, hairy cell leukemia, other MPNs in spent phaseTumor clusters in marrow; hairy cell = BRAF V600E, pancytopenia
Trap

Any MPN can end in a "spent," fibrotic phase that looks like PMF. Leukoerythroblastosis also occurs whenever marrow is infiltrated (metastatic cancer).

LO 8Natural history and treatment

Q1. How does each MPN progress, and how is it treated?
MPNCourseTreatment
CMLChronic phase (3–4-year median survival, pre-TKI) → accelerated phase in 50% (therapy failure, cytopenias, extra chromosome abnormalities, fibrosis) → blast crisis (AML 60%, ALL 30%)Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (imatinib): sustained remissions, few side effects, ↓ BCR-ABL+ cells, ↓ transformation; don't extinguish the stem cell; resistance → 2nd/3rd-gen TKIs. Potential cure: allogeneic stem cell transplant early in chronic phase
PVIndolent, progressive; untreated → death in months; treated ≈10-year survival; post-polycythemic spent phase (fibrosis, cytopenias); AML 2%Phlebotomy (↓ viscosity) + low-dose aspirin (prevent thrombosis); alkylators occasionally (↑ AML/NHL risk)
ETIndolent; long symptom-free intervals interrupted by thrombotic or hemorrhagic episodes; near-normal life expectancy; median survival 10–15 years; fibrosis or blast crisis <5%Younger asymptomatic may need none; if thrombosis: antimetabolites (hydroxyurea), gentle chemo, low-dose aspirin
PMFWorsening anemia and fibrosis; death from infection, thrombosis, bleeding; survival 3–5 years; AML 5–20%Mainly symptomatic (Step 1: JAK2 inhibitor ruxolitinib; transplant is the only cure)
High yield

Transformation to AML: PV 2% < ET <5% < PMF 5–20%; CML blast crisis is the rule without therapy.

In-house exam

Imatinib targets the ABL kinase from t(9;22). TKIs control counts and lower transformation risk but do not kill the stem cell.

Step 1

CML on imatinib for years now with CD19+ TdT+ blasts → lymphoid blast crisis (treat as ALL + TKI).

ApplyLO 8 application questions

A1Which MPN has the highest rate of transformation to AML?
Primary myelofibrosis (5–20%).
A2What two therapies form the base of PV treatment?
Phlebotomy and low-dose aspirin.

MCQExam-style questions

Score: 0 / 0

1A 59-year-old man has fatigue and early satiety. WBC 180,000 with myelocytes, metamyelocytes, bands and 8% basophils. No fever. Spleen 6 cm below the costal margin. Most likely genetic finding?

CML: Philadelphia chromosome.

2Which finding best favors a reactive neutrophilia over CML?

Reactive: <30k, bands, fever, no basophils, no spleen.

3What do the mutated tyrosine kinases of MPNs do to differentiation?

Maturation is effective → high peripheral counts.

4A 68-year-old man has headache, dizziness and hypertension. Hct 62%, O₂ saturation normal, serum EPO low. Most likely mutation?

PV: JAK2 >97%; low EPO separates it from secondary polycythemia.

5A 56-year-old woman has burning red fingers and toes. Platelets 850,000; BCR-ABL negative; ferritin and CRP normal. Marrow shows clusters of large atypical megakaryocytes. Diagnosis?

Erythromelalgia + sustained thrombocytosis + atypical megakaryocytes → ET.

6In primary myelofibrosis, which cells release the growth factors that drive marrow fibrosis?

Megakaryocyte PDGF and TGF-β stimulate fibroblasts to lay down collagen.

7A 69-year-old man has fatigue, abdominal fullness and recurrent infections. Smear: teardrop cells, nucleated RBCs and myelocytes. Marrow aspirate is a dry tap. Most likely diagnosis?

Leukoerythroblastosis + dacrocytes + fibrosis → PMF.

8A liver biopsy shows sinusoids filled with erythroid precursors, myeloid cells and megakaryocytes. What process is this?

EMH, classic for PMF.

9How does imatinib treat CML?

Targets the ABL kinase; controls counts but doesn't extinguish the stem cell.

10A patient with chronic-phase CML develops new lymphadenopathy, cytopenias and 25% blasts. What has happened?

Blast crisis: myeloid 60%, lymphoid 30%.

11Which therapy pair is first-line for polycythemia vera?

Phlebotomy lowers viscosity; aspirin prevents thrombosis.

12Which MPN is most likely to transform to AML?

PMF 5–20% vs PV 2% and ET <5%.
